chunks: ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm and Aḥmad ibn Mihrān, all together, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, from al-Ḥasan ibn Rāshid, from Yaʿqūb ibn Jaʿfar, who said:

I was with Abū Ibrāhīm (عليه السلام) when a man from the people of Najrān in Yemen, one of the monks, came to him, and with him was a nun. Al-Faḍl ibn Sawwār sought permission for them, so he said to him: “When tomorrow comes, bring them both to the well of Umm Khayr.” He said: We came the next day and found that the people had come as arranged. He ordered a mat of palm-leaf strips, then sat, and they sat. The nun began with questions and asked many questions, all of which he answered. Abū Ibrāhīm (عليه السلام) also asked her about things regarding which she had nothing, then she accepted Islam. Then the monk turned to question him, and he answered him regarding everything he asked.

The monk said: “I had been strong in my religion, and I left behind no one among the Christians on earth who reached my rank in knowledge. I had heard of a man in India who, whenever he wished, would make hajj to Bayt al-Maqdis in a day and a night, then return to his home in the land of India. So I asked about him, in which land he was, and it was said to me that he was in Subdhān. I asked the one who informed me, and he said: he knew the Name by which Āṣif, the companion of Sulaymān, prevailed when he brought the throne of Sabaʾ, and it is what Allah mentioned to you in your Book, and to us, the communities of religions, in our books.” Abū Ibrāhīm (عليه السلام) said to him: “How many Names belonging to Allah are there by which the supplicant is not turned back?” The monk said: “The Names are many; but as for the decreed ones among them, by which the supplicant is not turned back, they are seven.” Abū al-Ḥasan (عليه السلام) said to him: “Inform me about what you preserve of them.” The monk said: “No, by Allah who sent down the Tawrah upon Mūsā, and made ʿĪsā a lesson for the worlds and a trial for the gratitude of those possessed of intellect, and made Muḥammad a blessing and mercy, and made ʿAlī (عليه السلام) a lesson and insight, and made the awṣiyāʾ from his progeny and the progeny of Muḥammad—I do not know; and if I had known, I would not have needed your speech in it, nor come to you, nor ask you.”

Abū Ibrāhīm (عليه السلام) said to him: “Return to the account of the Indian.” The monk said to him: “I had heard of these Names, but I did not know their inner reality, nor their divisions; I did not know what they were, nor how they were, nor their supplications. So I set out until I arrived at Subdhān of India and asked about the man. It was said to me: he had built a monastery on a mountain, and he no longer came out nor was seen except twice every year. The people of India claimed that Allah had caused a spring to gush forth for him in his monastery, and they claimed that crops were grown for him without his casting seed, and land was tilled for him without any ploughing done by him. I came to his door and remained three days, neither knocking at the door nor trying to open it. Then when it was the fourth day, Allah opened the door, and a cow came bearing firewood, dragging her udder, with the milk in it almost flowing out. She pushed the door and it opened; I followed her and entered. I found the man standing, looking toward the sky and weeping, looking toward the earth and weeping, and looking toward the mountains and weeping.”

I said: “Glory be to Allah! How few are those like you in our age.” He said to me: “By Allah, I am only one good deed among the good deeds of a man whom you left behind you.” I said to him: “I was informed that you possess a Name from the Names of Allah by which you reach Bayt al-Maqdis every day and night, then return to your home.” He said to me: “Do you know Bayt al-Maqdis?” I said: “I know only the Bayt al-Maqdis that is in al-Shām.” He said: “It is not Bayt al-Maqdis; rather it is al-Bayt al-Muqaddas, and it is the house of the family of Muḥammad (صلى الله عليه وآله).” I said to him: “As for what I have heard until this day of mine, it is Bayt al-Maqdis.” He said to me: “Those were the prayer-niches of the prophets, and it used to be said of them: the enclosure of the prayer-niches, until the interval came that was between Muḥammad and ʿĪsā (صلوات الله عليهما), and affliction drew near from the people of shirk, and punishments settled in the dwellings of the devils; so they altered, changed, and transferred those names. And this is the word of Allah, blessed and exalted—the inward meaning concerns the family of Muḥammad, and the outward is a likeness:”
“They are nothing but names which you and your fathers have named; Allah has not sent down any authority for them.”

I said to him: “I have journeyed to you from a distant land, facing seas, griefs, worries, and fear, and morning and evening I had despaired lest I not attain my need.” He said to me: “I do not think your mother carried you except that a noble angel was present with her, and I know not that your father, when he intended intercourse with your mother, except that he had performed ghusl and came to her in a state of purity; and I only suppose that he had studied the fourth book during that night vigil of his, so a good ending was sealed for him. Return from where you came, then proceed until you arrive at the city of Muḥammad (صلى الله عليه وآله), which is called Ṭaybah, and whose name in the Jāhiliyyah had been Yathrib. Then go to a place there called al-Baqīʿ. Then ask about a house called Dār Marwān, and stay there for three days. Then ask about the black shaykh who is at its door making mats—and in their land that is called al-khaṣaf. Be gentle with the shaykh and say to him: ‘Your lodger who used to stay in the corner of the house containing the four pieces of wood has sent me to you.’ Then ask him about so-and-so son of so-and-so, and ask him where his gathering-place is, and ask him at what hour he passes there, so that he may show him to you or describe him to you, and you may recognize him by the description. And I shall describe him to you.” I said: “When I meet him, what shall I do?” He said: “Ask him about what has been and what is to be, and ask him about the landmarks of the religion of those who have passed and those who remain.”

Abū Ibrāhīm (عليه السلام) said to him: “Your companion whom you met gave you sincere counsel.” The monk said: “What is his name? May I be your ransom.” He said: “He is Mutammim ibn Fayrūz, and he is from the children of Persia. He is among those who believed in Allah alone, having no partner, and worshipped Him with sincerity and certitude, and fled from his people when he feared them. So his Lord granted him judgment, guided him to the path of rectitude, made him among the Godwary, and brought familiarity between him and His sincere servants. There is no year except that he visits Makkah in it as a pilgrim, and performs ʿumrah at the start of every month once, and comes from his place in India to Makkah as a grace and help from Allah. Thus does Allah reward the grateful.”

Then the monk asked him many questions, and he answered all of them. He also asked the monk about matters regarding which the monk had nothing, so he informed him of them. Then the monk said: “Inform me about eight letters that were sent down: four of them became manifest on earth, and four of them remained in the air. Upon whom were those four that are in the air sent down, and who will interpret them?” He said: “That is our Qāʾim; Allah will send it down upon him, so he will interpret it, and He will send down upon him what He did not send down upon the truthful ones, the messengers, and the guided ones.” Then the monk said: “Inform me about two of those four letters that are on earth—what are they?” He said: “I will inform you of all four of them. As for the first: there is no god but Allah alone, having no partner, everlasting. The second: Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وآله), in sincerity. The third: we are the Ahl al-Bayt. The fourth: our Shiʿah are from us, and we are from the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وآله), and the Messenger of Allah is from Allah by a cause.”

So the monk said to him: “I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, and that what he brought from Allah is true, and that you are the chosen ones of Allah from among His creation, and that your Shiʿah are the purified ones, the selected ones, and for them is Allah’s good end. And all praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.” Then Abū Ibrāhīm (عليه السلام) called for a khazz robe, a Qūhī shirt, a cloak, shoes, and a cap, and gave them to him. He performed the noon salat (prayer) and said to him: “Be circumcised.” He said: “I was circumcised in my seventh year.”

key_terms.آصَفُ: Āṣif, companion of Sulaymān, cited as one who knew a divine Name
key_terms.أَبُو إِبْرَاهِيمَ: Imam Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar (عليه السلام), the central figure answering the monk’s questions
key_terms.أَهْلُ الْبَيْتِ: The family of the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وآله), presented as a fundamental truth
key_terms.الرَّاهِبُ: The monk from Najrān who debates, inquires, and ultimately accepts Islam
key_terms.الِاسْمَ: The divine Name associated here with extraordinary efficacy and access to hidden realities
key_terms.الْبَيْتُ الْمُقَدَّسُ: In this context, identified as the house of Āl Muḥammad (صلى الله عليه وآله)
key_terms.شِيعَتُنَا: The Shiʿah of the Imams, described here as belonging to them
key_terms.قَائِمُنَا: The Qāʾim from Ahl al-Bayt who will interpret what remains hidden

ai.seo_question: How does Imam Mūsā al-Kāẓim (عليه السلام) describe the knowledge of the divine Names and the status of Ahl al-Bayt in this hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith narrates a lengthy encounter between Abū Ibrāhīm Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar (عليه السلام) and a monk and nun from Najrān, culminating in their recognition of his divinely granted knowledge and the monk’s acceptance of Islam. It includes themes of the divine Names, the virtues of Ahl al-Bayt, esoteric interpretation, and the future role of the Qāʾim in unveiling knowledge kept hidden.
